body:
The maintainer reported this in chat on 2026-11-16. His words: "its just to much compile in each "batch".. so it takes forever to get thru a post-merge-gate - even with -j6 set.. if u set a -j6.. there should be 2 cores per procss. so a max of 3 tests per batch.."

## What happens

- `xtask/src/plan.rs` gives each cargo step `-j 6` and `--test-threads=6` (`J`, `T`).
- `xtask/src/lanes.rs` runs up to `LIMIT = 4` steps at the same time in the release tier.
- Each lane keeps the full `-j 6` and `--test-threads=6`. Four lanes thus start up to 24 compile jobs and 24 test threads.
- The gate also shares its machine with review builds and worker builds. Each of those uses `-j 6` too.
- The result is more jobs than cores. Each lane is slower than a serial run.

## What to do

1. Make the job count one budget for the whole gate (default 6). Read it from one constant, with an environment override.
2. When N lanes run at the same time, give each lane `-j (budget / N)` and `--test-threads=(budget / N)`, minimum 1.
3. Set the lane limit from the budget: at most `budget / 2` lanes. With a budget of 6 this is 3 lanes with 2 jobs each.
4. A step that runs alone keeps the full budget.
5. Print the budget, the lane count and the jobs for each lane at the start of the gate.
6. Apply the same rule to each tier that runs lanes, and to #1941 if it adds lanes to the quick and batch tiers.
7. Update the `gate` skill and the `runners` skill: the sum of `-j` of all builds on one machine stays at or below its core count.

## Done means

- A unit test in `xtask` shows that the sum of `-j` in each wave is at or below the budget, and that no wave has more than `budget / 2` lanes.
- A unit test shows that a step that runs alone gets the full budget.
- `cargo xtask gate release --dry-run` prints the budget and the jobs for each lane.
- The PR body has the wall time of one batch run and one release wave, before and after.
- The PR body has the line `Process change: yes`.

## What is missing

An operation has no way to name model faces or edges that the tool must not touch. The user cannot protect a finished surface, a datum face or a sharp edge from a later operation.

## What to do

1. Add a "Do not touch" selection to the Boundaries group of the Geometry tab of an operation.
   - The user picks faces and edges in the viewport.
   - Each picked item shows as a row with a remove button.
   - The viewport shows the protected items in a different colour while the operation is selected.
2. Store the selection on the operation. The change goes through an undoable command (AGENTS.md "Everything Is a Command"). The command ships with its MCP tool.
3. Add a clearance parameter (default 0, the stock to leave still applies). The tool stays this distance from each protected item.
4. Each generator that the operation type uses keeps the tool clear of the protected items. This includes the cutting moves, the lead moves, the link moves and the plunges. The check uses the full tool: flutes, shank and holder.
5. The verify gate checks each generated move against the protected items. This check is independent of the generator.
6. If a move touches a protected item, the operation is refused or marked "incomplete" with a diagnostic that names the item. The post is blocked. The program is never posted with such a move (AGENTS.md "Prime Directive: Never Crash, Never Gouge").
7. If a protected item is also in the machining selection of the same operation, refuse the selection when the command is created. Say which item is in the two lists.
8. The project file stores the selection. Say in the PR if older builds refuse the new file.

## Scope

- First slice: the selection, the command, the MCP tool, the verify check and the refusal, for one 2D and one 3D operation type. The PR names the two types.
- Later slices: the other operation types. File one issue for each family (2D, 3D, multi-axis, turning, wire).
- Reference material is public machining literature and published user documentation at behaviour level only (AGENTS.md "Clean-Room Protocol"). Write the labels in our own words.

## Safety

This work is under the safety floor. It adds a gouge law and can change posted G-code for an operation that has protected items. An operation without protected items must give the same toolpath as before: pin that.

## Done means

- The Geometry tab has the "Do not touch" selection under Boundaries, with pick, list and remove.
- Undo and redo restore the selection. The MCP tool sets and reads it.
- A test with a protected face next to the cut region shows that no move comes nearer than the clearance.
- A test with a protected face that the selected region cannot avoid shows the refusal, with the item named, and a blocked post.
- A test shows that an operation without protected items gives a toolpath that does not change.
- The structural UI test asserts the new rows and their labels.
- The user guide describes the selection and the refusal.

- The application has an editor for post scripts (`.cps`).
- The user starts from a blank template. A blank template posts nothing.
- The user selects a sample program, for example a standard 2D operation. The editor runs the temporary script on that sample and shows the G-code.

- The editor has a library of common snippets. The user inserts a snippet and changes it.
- The editor is a panel of its own. The user can close all other panels to give it the room.

2. Which sample programs does the editor offer? Recorded `.cl` files (for example from `crates/app/tests/golden/`) need no generator and no open project. Is "the operations of the open project" a second source?

- Then this issue is closed.

body:
Part of #1490.

The rest generator currently trusts an entered previous tool. It assumes that tool cut the pocket to the requested depth.

Add a previous-operations mode that derives remaining material from the stock those operations actually leave.

Design decision:
- Keep the entered-tool mode explicit. Add a separate previous-operations mode through an undoable command, the project file, and MCP.
- Read only earlier operations in the same setup, in their actual order. Reuse the established carried-stock infrastructure.
- Require current operation paths and compatible setup coordinates. Refuse missing, stale, or unsupported stock by name, or mark the result incomplete.
- Read remaining stock at every requested cut depth. A shallow roughing pass does not prove that the lower floor is clear.
- Include tool shape, wall and floor allowances, and the supported simulation resolution. Unknown cells remain occupied.
- Pass a conservative remaining-material region to the motion generator. Do not infer cleared volume from the previous tool diameter alone.
- Invalidate the result when an earlier operation changes, moves, is suppressed, or changes its tool or depth.
- Keep the current stock backend. Do not combine this feature with the field-engine migration in #586 or #637.

Tests:
- Compare the rest region with independently simulated earlier operations.
- Test mixed previous tool sizes, bull-nose tools, partial depths, wall allowances, islands, and disconnected cuts.
- Test missing paths, stale paths, operation reordering, changed tools, and unsupported stock frames.
- Prove the plan never removes material from its rest estimate unless the earlier cuts prove that material absent.
- Prove command undo, project save and reopen, MCP editing, and dependency invalidation.
- Remove each depth and stock-validity guard separately. Each mutation must fail its pinning test.

Done means: previous-operations mode uses conservative stock at each depth, passes these tests, and never guesses when stock cannot be established.

Related: #586 and #637 migrate the stock representation. This issue consumes the current representation for 2D rest machining.

Literature: M. Held, On the Computational Geometry of Pocket Machining, LNCS 500 (1991), https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/3-540-54103-9. Z. Yao, S. K. Gupta and D. S. Nau, Algorithms for selecting cutters in multi-part milling problems, Computer-Aided Design 35 (2003), https://www.cs.umd.edu/~nau/papers/yao2003algorithms.pdf.

These sources describe pocket geometry and cutter coverage. The per-depth stock and invalidation contract above is this project's decision. Do not copy another CAM product's code or output.

body:
Part of #1490.

The current rest pass plunges at each rest area. PR #1817 measures two corner entries per level that touch rest material at the cutter rim.

Implement entry from proved cleared space, followed by a feed into the rest area.

Design decision:
- Use conservative stock from the previous operations at the entry's actual depth.
- Prove clearance for the full cutter footprint throughout the descent and the lateral approach.
- Do not accept a clear tool axis as proof of a clear cutter rim.
- Keep unknown stock occupied. Account for simulation resolution and tool geometry in the clearance margin.
- Keep the approach inside the legal cutter-center region. Check islands, walls, stock, fixtures, and the supported tool envelope.
- Refuse the requested cleared-space entry by name when no proved route exists. Do not silently use an assumed entry hole.
- Keep ordinary cutting entry available as an explicit separate choice. Do not change its behavior as part of this task.

Tests:
- Reuse the 60 x 40 pocket with 3 mm corners, a 12 mm roughing tool, and a 4 mm rest tool from PR #1817.
- Require the full cutter footprint to remain clear during descent. Measure stock contact during the lateral cutting feed separately.
- Test shallow roughing, a bull-nose previous tool, islands, disconnected cleared regions, and insufficient entry room.
- Require named refusals for missing or stale stock and unsupported depth.
- Remove each footprint, depth, and stock-validity guard separately. Each mutation must fail its pinning test.

Done means: the fixture enters without plunging its rim into rest material, passes verification, and refuses every unproved entry case by name.

Related: #1816 reduces air cutting on the inner legs of corner rings. This issue changes the entry, not those ring legs.

Literature: M. Held, On the Computational Geometry of Pocket Machining, LNCS 500 (1991), https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/3-540-54103-9. Z. Yao, S. K. Gupta and D. S. Nau, Algorithms for selecting cutters in multi-part milling problems, Computer-Aided Design 35 (2003), https://www.cs.umd.edu/~nau/papers/yao2003algorithms.pdf.

These sources describe pocket geometry and cutter coverage. The full-footprint entry proof above is this project's decision. Do not copy another CAM product's code or output.

body:
The depth ladder of the depth-stepping operations keeps the remainder in the last step. Some users expect equal steps.

What happens:

- The shared level law `camcraft_motion::machining2d::cut_levels` steps down by the full stepdown from Top Z.
- The last level ends at Bottom Z exactly. The last step is the remainder.
- Example: Top Z 20, Bottom Z 2, stepdown 5 gives the levels `[15, 10, 5, 2]`. The last step is 3 mm. The other steps are 5 mm.

The other choice:

- Equal steps: the same number of levels, `ceil(span / stepdown)`, and each step is `span / count`.
- The same example gives four steps of 4.5 mm: `[15.5, 11, 6.5, 2]`.
- Each step stays at or below the stepdown. The load on the tool is more equal, and the last pass is not a light rub.

Where it came from: found while fixing #2004 (the ladder now starts one stepdown under Top Z). The fix kept the remainder and recorded this choice in `docs/decisions/2004-top-z-level.md`, decision 7.

body:
The maintainer reported this in chat on 2026-11-15, on v0.21.0, with a screenshot of a 2D Adaptive operation.

His words: "a common issue i see is that the first toolpath is always ontop of the part at TopZ ... even thos stepdown states "full depth" of the cut.. technically it should just be one single toolpath right?" and "find it in all operations.. This is a high effortf, P2 bug.."

## What happens

The operation has Top Z = 13 (stock top + 1), Bottom Z = 0 and Stepdown = 50 mm. It posts two full levels: one at Z 13 and one at Z 0. The level at Top Z cuts no material. It doubles the cycle time of a one-level cut.

## Cause

The shared level law starts its list at Top Z:

```rust
// crates/motion/src/machining2d/levels.rs, cut_levels
let mut z = top;
while z > bottom + tol {
    zs.push(z);      // the first level is `top`
    z -= stepdown;
}
zs.push(bottom);
```

`cut_levels(13, 0, 50)` gives `[13, 0]`. The correct list is `[0]`. With a stepdown of 5 it gives `[13, 8, 3, 0]`. The correct list is `[8, 3, 0]`.

`crates/app/src/operation/area.rs` `ladder_planes` restates the same law, and its unit test pins the wrong list (`ladder_planes(20.0, 0.0, 5.0) == [20, 15, 10, 5, 0]`).

## Callers found (read-only search, not complete)

- `crates/motion/src/machining2d/`: `adaptive_troch.rs:158`, `bore.rs:308`, `circular.rs:278` and `:280`, `contour_params.rs:216` (2D Contour), `face.rs:156`, `pocket.rs:277`, `pocket_hsm.rs:49` and `pocket_troch.rs:68` (level counts for the budget), `slots.rs:160` and `:343`, `trochoid_slot.rs:319`
- `crates/motion/src/machining3d/entry.rs:89`, `:123`, `:236`, `:258` (3D Pocket and its rest pass)
- `crates/app/src/operation/area.rs:74`, `:182`, `:233` (`ladder_planes`, the 3D pocket region build)
- `crates/motion/tests/control_comp.rs` (a test helper with the same name)

Not yet read: `crates/motion/src/finishing3d/ladder.rs` `levels`, `crates/motion/src/machining2d/contour_depth.rs` `ladder`, `crates/motion/src/machining3d/ladder.rs`, the turning, drilling (peck), engraving, chamfer, plasma and EDM depth ladders, and each operation with its own loop.

## For the work

1. Audit each operation of each machine type for a level at Top Z (or at the material top) that removes no material. List each in the PR with the result.
2. Fix the shared law so that the first level is `top - stepdown`, and the last level is `bottom` exactly. Use one law: `ladder_planes` in `app` must use the motion law, or match it by a shared test.
3. Check the special cases:
   - Top Z below the stock top (material above Top Z): no level may cut more than one stepdown. Find what each operation means by Top Z, and state it.
   - `circular.rs:278` starts at a previous level (`cut_levels(prev, floor, ...)`): make sure that it does not cut the previous level two times.
   - Face: a single pass at `cut_z` stays one pass.
   - A stepdown of 0 or a span of 0: the current refusal and the one-plane result stay.
   - Rest machining and the 3D Pocket shell levels: the level count and the budget readings change. Restate the budget pins with the reason.
   - The ramp, helix and plunge entries that read `top_z` as the material top (`Motion::top_z`) must stay correct.
4. The size of the last step (the remainder or equal steps) is a separate choice. Keep the current remainder rule, and file a follow-up issue for the choice.

This changes posted G-code for existing projects (one level fewer for each depth-stepping operation). It is under the safety floor.

## Done means

- No operation posts a level at Top Z that removes no material when Top Z is at or above the material top.
- One-level case: Top Z 13, Bottom Z 0, Stepdown 50 gives one level at Z 0. Pinned for 2D Adaptive, 2D Pocket, 2D Contour, Slot, Bore, Circular and 3D Pocket.
- Multi-level case: Top Z 20, Bottom Z 0, Stepdown 5 gives `[15, 10, 5, 0]`. Pinned on the shared law and on `ladder_planes`.
- Each changed golden is listed in the PR with the reason. The PR says that posted G-code changes.
- Each verify and gouge pin of the touched operations stays green.

body:
Design 5-axis kinematics and Haas NGC multi-axis posting for trunnion tables (`TR160`, `TR210`, `TRT100`) and universal machining centers (`UMC-500`).

Public Haas specifications and codebase behavior expose these open problems:
- **Kinematics mismatch in CamCraft:** `crates/cl/src/cl/pose.rs:53` (`axis_to_angles`) outputs `[A, B, 0.0]` with `C` always zero, and `crates/app/src/machine/judge.rs:79-105` checks literal rotary letters without inverse kinematics. A `UMC-500` uses `B` (+120° to -35°) plus `C` (360°), which fails when any Y-tilted pose requests `A`. A `TR160`/`TRT100` calls its cradle `A` (±120°) and platter `B` (360°), where platter `B` turns perpendicular to tilted `A` rather than around static Y.
- **NGC 5-axis G-codes and options:** Haas NGC uses `G254`/`G255` (Dynamic Work Offset) for 3+2 indexing and `G234` (Tool Center Point Control, not Fanuc `G43.4`) for simultaneous 4/5-axis cutting. Both `G254` and `G234` are paid options (`haascnc.com`); controls without TCPC require `G93` inverse-time feed (`F = 1 / minutes` per move).
- **Brakes and limits:** 4th-axis (`M10`/`M11`) and 5th-axis (`M12`/`M13`) brakes clamp during indexed cuts and stay released (`M11`/`M13`) during simultaneous motion.

Deliver a design decision in `docs/decisions/` covering:
1. Inverse kinematics or kinematic-chain representation in `cl`/`judge.rs` for `B+C` UMCs and `A+B` trunnions (`TR160`/`TRT100`).
2. Option-gating rules in `.mch` and `haas.cps` for `G254`/`G255` (DWO), `G234` (TCPC), `G93` fallback, and `M10`–`M13` brakes.
3. Concrete implementation sub-issues for machine definitions, IK checks, and `haas.cps` 5-axis output.

Done means: A design decision in `docs/decisions/` defines the kinematic model, option gating, and implementation split for Haas 5-axis support.

body:
## What happens

2D Contour with Side Auto on a picked rim of a BLIND bore resolves to Outside. The Outside ring stands in the part below the mouth. Before #1927 the operation cut only the top plane (in air) and posted with no warning. With the #1927 fix (PR on `issue/1927-contour-outside-hole-refusal`) the operation is refused by name ("set Side to Inside").

Fixture: `testdata/models/Milling-test.step`, the closed rim chain of radius 12.5 at Z 20. Test: `crates/app/tests/area_open.rs`, `a_containment_that_puts_the_tool_in_the_part_is_refused_by_name` (the last assert pins the refusal).

## Cause

`selection_geometry_impl` (`crates/app/src/operation/selection.rs`) resolves Auto by the fill ratio: the area of the ring that is part material, read from the part's XY silhouette. The floor of a blind bore fills the silhouette inside the rim. Thus the fill is near 1 and Auto selects Outside. A through hole has an empty silhouette inside the rim, so Auto selects Inside there.

## Done means

- Auto reads the material that the ring bounds at the ring's own level (or just below it), not the full XY silhouette.
- Auto on a blind bore rim resolves to Inside and cuts the wall from inside.
- The last assert of the test above changes to a clean Inside path.
- Auto on a boss and on an outer wall still resolves to Outside.

## Workaround

Set Side to Inside.

title: post-merge.yml: let a running post-merge gate finish (cancel-in-progress: false), so a merge batch still gets complete results

labels.name: area:build
labels.description: Build, CI, release, tests

labels.name: in-review
labels.description: Fix pushed on a branch with an open PR; merges at the next cut

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:low

labels.name: P5
labels.description: Agent surface and tooling keep up with what shipped

body:
**The request (mkinney, 2026-11-15):** make sure the post-merge gate runs to completion even when more merges arrive, using the one-line change below.

## What happens

`.github/workflows/post-merge.yml`:

```yaml
concurrency:
  group: post-merge-${{ github.event_name == 'push' && 'main' || inputs.ref || 'main' }}
  cancel-in-progress: true
```

Each PR merge is its own push to main and starts its own run. With `cancel-in-progress: true`, each new merge cancels the run in progress. In a merge batch (N merges within one gate run, about 37 min), only the LAST run finishes:
- #1752: seven runs in a row were cancelled by later merges. The breaking merge had to be found by hand in a range of 6 merges, including the cut merge.
- #1909 and #1856 (2026-11-15): after the 10-PR bulk batch, the only result was for the tip. Each needed a manual search for the cause (#1839, and #1787 with #1793).

## Proposal (one line)

```yaml
  cancel-in-progress: false
```

With a concurrency group, GitHub keeps at most one run in progress and one pending:
- The run already in progress always finishes. It gives a full result for its commit.
- A newer merge waits as the single pending run. A still newer merge replaces it, so runs do not pile up.

For a batch of N merges this tests 2 points (the first merge and the last), not 1. Each run gives a result. The cost: more runner time on the self-hosted post-merge runner (no billed minutes), and the result for the batch tip arrives up to one gate-run later.

The comment at the top of the file (line 9, "tests only the newest head (cancel-in-progress)") must change with it. The cut-skip logic (`post-merge-skip.sh`) does not change.

## Later options (not part of this issue)

- A unique group per commit (no cancels at all): every merge is tested, but a 10-PR batch takes about 6 h on one runner.
- Bisect-when-red: when a run fails, test the merges between the last green run and this one, to find the breaking merge automatically.

## Done means

`cancel-in-progress: false` is on the post-merge concurrency group, the comment explains the queue behaviour, and a batch of merges shows the in-progress run finishing (not "cancelled") in the Actions history.

A `.github/` workflow change: the maintainer's decision. Agents do not edit it.

body:
Found during #1842.

## What happens

With "Threading: G76 cycle" and a flank infeed, the Fanuc lathe post writes one G76 cycle. Two published manuals show that the control ends every pass at the programmed end point D:

- FANUC Series 0i-F lathe operator's manual B-64604EN-1, section 4.2.7, Fig. 4.2.7 (a).
- Siemens SINUMERIK ISO Turning programming manual A5E52211627B, Fig. 4-25.

The turning kernel (`crates/motion/src/turning/thread.rs`, the pass loop) shifts the start AND the end of each pass by the same flank offset. Thus a shallower pass ends short of D by `(k - depth) * tan(a/2)`. Only the root pass ends at D.

## Effect

The control cuts each shallower pass a little longer than the laid pass that the verdict and the stock simulation see. The extra length is at a smaller depth, inside the groove that the root pass cuts to D. It removes no material beyond the root pass and does not move toward a shoulder. Thus this is not a wrong-output defect. But the simulated passes are not exactly the passes that run.

body:
**The request (mkinney, 2026-11-15):** "Do we need to handle svg file import?" ... "Yes file it". Many waterjet, laser and plasma users draw in Inkscape or Illustrator and export SVG. WAZER's own app takes SVG and DXF (see #1525).

## What

Import an SVG file as 2D sketch geometry for 2D operations (Contour, Pocket, Engrave/Trace, plasma or waterjet profile). It goes into the same sketch entity as the DXF import, so the operations need no new input path.

## Depends on

- #1860 (DXF core reader), #1861 (2D sketch chaining, outer-vs-hole nesting, open chains) and #1862 (the sketch ECS entity, .camproj persistence, undoable import).
- Stack on those: the SVG reader only produces sketch chains and reuses chaining, nesting and the import command.

## Scope

- **Elements:** `path` (M/L/H/V/C/S/Q/T/A/Z, absolute and relative), `line`, `polyline`, `polygon`, `rect` (with rx/ry), `circle`, `ellipse`. `g` groups with `transform` (matrix, translate, scale, rotate, skew), applied to the geometry.
- **Curves:** cubic and quadratic Béziers and elliptical arcs become arcs or polylines within the document's chord tolerance. An arc stays an arc where it is circular after the transform.
- **Units and scale:** `width`/`height` with units (mm, cm, in, pt, pc, px), and the `viewBox`. px uses 96 px/in (the CSS rule). If the file states no physical size, the import asks for the scale. It never guesses silently.
- **Y axis:** SVG Y points down. Flip it so the drawing appears as it does in the editor.
- **Ignored, with a note:** fill, stroke style, text (unless converted to paths), images, clip paths, masks, `use` references to symbols outside the file.
- **Refusals, by name:** a malformed path, a zero or negative size, a degenerate arc, and a file larger than the import budget give a clear error, never a panic (the Prime Directive).
- **MCP:** an `import_svg` tool, or the shared sketch-import tool with format svg (AGENTS.md "Commands ship with an MCP tool").

## Not in scope (later)

- Text to outlines (fonts), embedded images, and CSS stylesheets.

## Done means

- A fixture SVG set (a rectangle with a hole, Bézier and arc shapes, a nested group with transforms, mm and in documents, and one file without a physical size) imports to the expected sketch chains. The tests pin the chain count, closure, nesting and size within tolerance.
- A 2D Contour on an imported SVG posts. A golden is pinned for one plasma or waterjet-style profile.
- Malformed fixtures are refused by name and never panic. The importer fuzz test covers the SVG reader.
- The user guide import page (and #1525's waterjet notes) lists SVG.

title: Mask tests: compare a generated toolpath with its described shape

labels.name: enhancement

body:
The maintainer asked for this in chat (2026-11-15):

> is it possible to use the cli tool to verify tool paths "visually".. we know what they should look like mathematically.. could we inspect them using rasterized tests?

> Idea is to sanity checks that changes to the motion crates actually gets implemented as described by the user

## Problem

A change to a toolpath generator is described in words in its issue (for example "the pass extends to the stock edge", "the corners are arcs", "the slot is cleared with trochoidal loops"). The tests of the change pin numbers that the author chose. No test compares the shape of the generated toolpath with the shape that the description gives. A change can pass its tests and not do what the user described.

## Proposal

Add a test helper that compares two masks on one grid:

- The expected region. The test builds it from the mathematical description (an outline, a depth, an extension).
- The swept region. The helper builds it from the tool footprint along the generated toolpath.

The helper gives these assertions:

- No overcut: no swept cell is outside the expected region, within one cell.
- Bounded leftover: the uncut area is below a stated limit, and the uncut cells are only in stated places.
- Engagement: no move cuts a width larger than the stated stepover.
- Shape laws: symmetry for a symmetric region, and no move outside the stock plus the stated extension.

When an assertion fails, the helper writes the difference mask as a PNG file into the test output folder. A person can then see where the toolpath is wrong. The test result comes from the numbers, not from an image comparison. No PNG golden is stored.

## Rules

- The helper is test code. It does not change a generator, a gouge check or a collision check.
- The helper is in the crate that owns the toolpath types (`crates/motion`), and uses the CPU rasteriser or its own grid. It does not need a GPU.
- The grid limits the precision to one cell. Exact laws (arc radius, depth, feed words) stay as numeric tests.
- A PR that changes a 2D generator in `crates/motion` adds or updates one mask test that states the described shape.

## First users

- Trochoidal slot.
- 2D Adaptive.
- The open-edge region of issue 1735 and the Slot extension of issue 1731.

Done means: the helper is in the repository with its own unit tests; the trochoidal slot and 2D Adaptive each have one mask test that fails when the generator is changed to overcut or to leave too much material (shown by a mutation check in the PR); a failed assertion writes the difference PNG; AGENTS.md "Testing" names the helper.

Part of #1446 (first slice: the motion-crate generator, `camcraft_motion::machining2d::rest_plan` / `rest_pocket`, on branch `issue/1446-rest-2d`).

Asked for by the maintainer (2026-11-13, quoted on #1446): "We wanna cover some of the toolpaths and things like that at first." and "Lets create issues on your suggestions, they made sense." Sources as he asked: "We should use perplexity to find literature on those types of toolpaths and not copy them straight up".

What the first slice leaves out of the generator, each of which needs design before code:

1. **2D Adaptive over a rest area.** `rest_pocket` refuses the Adaptive strategy by name. The adaptive plan picks its own entry and bounds engagement assuming a full pocket; over a rest area the entry should stand in cleared floor and the engagement model must know what is already cut.
2. **Entry from already-cut space.** The first slice plunges into each rest area like a plain pocket, so nothing depends on the cleared-area estimate. Entering sideways from cleared floor is faster, and makes that estimate safety-critical: the cleared area must be read small (it is today) and the entry refused, by name, where it cannot be proved.
3. **The previous tool from the previous operations.** Today the previous tool is entered by hand and trusted (the path says so in a note). The issue also asks for "from previous operations": the cleared area measured from the stock the earlier operations of the setup leave, including their depth - a rest pass must not assume a depth the roughing never reached. Where the carried stock cannot be established, refuse by name or mark incomplete; never guess.
4. **Zigzag.** Refused by name in the first slice because rows leave cusps along the walls of a rest area. A row plan with a closing ring per rest area would lift the refusal.

Literature to start from (cited in the first slice): Held, "On the Computational Geometry of Pocket Machining", LNCS 500, 1991; Veeramani and Gau, Computer-Aided Design 29(12), 1997, and IIE Transactions 32, 2000; Yao, Gupta and Nau, Computer-Aided Design 35(9), 2003. No code or text from any other CAM product (Clean-Room Protocol).

Done means: each of the four is either built with its pinning tests (verifier clean, no rapid into material the cleared-area reading cannot prove cut, refusals named) or split into its own issue with a recorded decision; the literature used is cited in the PR.

body:
Asked for by the maintainer (2026-11-13, in chat): "We should be able to load DXF file to do profile cuts on."

What is missing: the importers read solid and mesh models only. A 2D drawing (a DXF from a CAD or sheet-metal program) cannot be loaded, so a flat part cannot be profiled without first being modelled as a solid. No DXF code exists in the tree today; issues 743 and 744 want DXF for tool and fixture profiles and can share this reader.

Wanted:
- A DXF reader for the 2D entities that carry a profile: LINE, ARC, CIRCLE, LWPOLYLINE and POLYLINE (with bulges), ELLIPSE and SPLINE (flattened within a tolerance, arcs kept as arcs where they are arcs). Units from `$INSUNITS`, with a question to the user when the file states none (never a silent guess between mm and inch). Layers are kept, so the user can pick by layer. Blocks/INSERT are expanded or refused by name; text, dimensions and hatches are skipped and counted in the import summary.
- The drawing loads as sketch geometry on the setup's XY plane: shown in the viewport, placed with the stock, saved in the project file.
- Chaining: touching entities are joined into chains within a tolerance; closed chains are told from open ones, and outer loops from holes.
- The 2D operations (2D Contour first; Pocket, Slot, Engrave and the plasma/laser profile operations after) take those chains as their geometry selection, with side (inside/outside) and direction per chain, exactly as they take model edges today.
- Loading is an undoable command with its MCP tool (Everything Is a Command; commands ship with an MCP tool). Model > Open offers `.dxf`, and so does the viewport drop of issue 1450.

Safety:
- The reader is an importer of untrusted files: malformed group codes, truncated files, NaN or huge coordinates, zero-length entities and self-intersecting loops give a clean error or a named skip, never a crash or a hang; it gets a fuzz test like the other importers.
- A gap wider than the chaining tolerance leaves an open chain that is shown as open; it is never closed silently, and an inside/outside cut on an open chain is refused by name.
- A flattened spline or ellipse stays within the stated tolerance of the drawn curve, pinned by a test, so the cut part is to size.
- Units are part of the result: the import summary states them, and a wrong-unit part (25.4 times too big or small) cannot happen without the user having answered the question.

Sources: the DXF format from Autodesk's published DXF reference (a public file-format document; format only), written from scratch or through a permissively licensed crate if one fits (a new dependency needs the maintainer's yes and a `docs/decisions/` entry). No DXF sample files taken from another product's install tree.

Scope note: this is larger than one PR. Suggested split when it is picked up: (1) reader + fuzz test in the geometry crate, (2) sketch entity, project file and viewport display, (3) chaining and selection in 2D Contour, (4) the other 2D operations.

Done means: a DXF with an outer rectangle, two circles and a slot made of lines and arcs loads, shows in the viewport and survives save/reopen; a 2D Contour picks the outer loop (outside) and the holes (inside) and posts a program whose golden CL matches the drawn sizes; a file with no units asks; an open chain is shown and refused for a side-compensated cut; a corrupt DXF gives a named error; the fuzz test runs; undo removes the drawing; the MCP tool loads a DXF headlessly.

The gouge laws of the upright mill kinds subtract the excess from their tolerance while a positive tolerance is left: the section law (b), the solid law (b2), the envelope law's gouge half (f), `generate::contain_into`, the lathe's axial hole verdict, and the program sim's deviation tolerance. Past that, the program gate refuses by name.

**What is owed.** Everything below is safe today (refused, or stricter than before), but less useful than it should be.

1. **Kinds refused outright on any reduced-fidelity model**, because their gouge laws do not read the excess yet (`operation::fidelity_law::excess_aware`):
   - the cone and engrave rides: 2D chamfer, deburr, trace, engrave (generator construction laws);
   - probe, and the cross drill (`operation/cross_part.rs`, `SolidLaw { allow: GOUGE_TOL }`);
   - the multi-axis kinds (`motion` `multiaxis/entry_ramp.rs`, `stamp*.rs`, `rotary_links.rs`) and the rotary kinds (`operation/rotary_law.rs`, `allow` and `rapid_allow`);
   - turning (`motion` `turning/revolve.rs`, `form.rs`, `thread.rs`; `blade_warnings`, `thread_warnings`, `form_warnings`);
   - plasma.
   Each needs `material.excess` threaded into its law and the kind added to `excess_aware`. A metre-unit STEP file is always reduced fidelity (next point), so these kinds cannot post on one today.
2. **Collision laws are not tightened**: shank and holder reach (`sim` `verify/reach.rs`), rapids in stock (`verify/rapids.rs`, `rapids_posed.rs`, `rapids_radial.rs`), the turning rapid, bar-feed and holder scans (`margin: GOUGE_TOL` in `generate.rs`). They judge clearance against rest material. While an operation still posts the excess is under 0.01 mm, so a clearance can read up to that much too generous on a convex wall.
3. **A metre-unit STEP file** stops at the kernel's least tolerance (1e-5 m = 0.01 mm, #839) and is flagged reduced fidelity with half the verdict tolerance left. Scaling the geometry to millimetres before meshing would remove the cause.
4. **The facet budget is not a user setting.** The refusal says "re-import with a larger budget" (the maintainer's wording on #864), but `MAX_FACETS` is a constant. The import dialog, the script verb and MCP `import_model` need a budget the user can raise.
5. **Display tolerances** still read the plain 0.01 mm on a reduced-fidelity model: the machined-surface classes (`machined_classes.rs`) and the viewport preview (`ui` `trace/eye.rs`, `cpu_eye.rs`). The binding verdict is tightened; the colours are not.
6. **The envelope law (f) and the containment solid law** are tightened through the same helper as (b) but have no fixture-level pin of their own on a reduced-fidelity model.

Done means: each kind in (1) is either judged with tightened laws or stays refused for a stated reason; the laws in (2) grow their bands by the excess; (3) and (4) are decided and built or closed with the reason; pins for (6).

body:
A tool can't store a part number, vendor, coating, helix or free-text notes.

**Where:** `ToolDto` (`crates/app/src/project/file.rs:292`) has no free-text or vendor fields.

**Effect:** tool libraries built from catalogs have to cram the part number, coating and other facts into the tool's name, e.g. `<vendor> <part#> 1/4" 4FL flat AlTiN LOC 3/4 OAL 2-1/2`. They can't be searched, sorted or shown in a setup sheet's tool list. Reordering a tool means reading the name.

**Fix:** optional fields `part_number`, `vendor`, `coating`, `helix_deg` and `notes` on the tool, as an additive key so old files load unchanged. Show them in the tool editor and on the setup sheet's tool list, and add them to MCP.

Effort: medium (data only, no geometry).

**Done means:** the fields round-trip through `.camproj` and `.camtools`, show on the setup sheet, and are editable via UI and MCP; pinned.

body:
There's no thread-mill tool kind.

**Where:** `ToolKind` (`crates/tools/src/tools.rs:23`) has `Tap` and the lathe `Thread` insert, but no single-form or multi-form thread mill.

**Effect:** thread milling is a common job on small CNC mills (interpolated threads in any material, large or odd sizes, no tap breakage). A vendor tool library can't carry thread mills at all. In one real catalog build, over 300 thread mills had to be left out.

**Fix sketch:**
- New kinds: single-form (one tooth, any pitch within range) and multi-form (several teeth, a fixed pitch). Each carries cutter diameter, form angle, pitch or pitch range, teeth count, neck and shank.
- A thread-milling operation: helical interpolation, internal and external, climb or conventional, single or multi pass, radial passes.
- Simulation and gouge laws for the form.

Effort: max (a new kind, a helical op and the sim).

**Done means:** a thread mill can be stored and used by a thread-milling op that verifies clean and posts helical G2/G3 with Z; pinned with goldens.

body:
Follow-up from #786, part of #131.

**What happens today:** #786 made `spindle.rigid_tapping` a validated `.mch` capability, and the program gate refuses tap cycles by name on any machine that states `false`. Every Tormach mill and router file states it. The three Tormach lathe files (`tormach-8l.mch`, `tormach-15l-slant-pro.mch`, `tormach-15lx-slant-pro.mch`) don't state it, so they read as "not limited". The public material found during #786 didn't settle whether these lathes rigid-tap: PathPilot release notes mention a G84 tapping cycle but don't tie it to a lathe model and spindle.

**Expected:** each Tormach lathe file states `rigid_tapping` as its operator manual documents it (behaviour only, clean room), with the source cited in a `docs/decisions/` entry. If the manuals still don't settle it, say so on this issue and leave the files unstated.

**Done means:**
- The 8L, 15L Slant-PRO and 15LX Slant-PRO files each state `rigid_tapping` from a cited public source, or this issue records why they can't.
- `every_tormach_mill_and_router_file_states_rigid_tapping` in `crates/app/tests/rigid_tapping.rs` is widened to cover the lathes.

Effort: high, under the safety floor (it decides whether a G84 is posted).

- change/remember the output folder
- override the units of measure (inches/mm)
- add chip conveyor info (idle time, run time, use chip transport)
